messages.subject: Re: Multi state model - imputation
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

In my experience, with lots and lots of NAs, mixing of chains isn't as good as when there's no or few NAs. So if you have a few NAs in your response, it's all good, but it's best to avoid data with lots of NAs.

messages.subject: Re: Initial values have strong influence on posterior in community occupancy model
messages.subject_clean: Initial values have strong influence on posterior in community occupancy model
messages.body_plain:
What initial values are you providing for w and Z? Any chance you are supplying initial values for latent states which aren't getting sampled by the model? If some latent states aren't getting sampled by the model, they will just remain with the initial values you provided, thereby giving very different output.

> Hello,
> After sen your code, I can see that there are a lot of parameters on it and as Marc wrote this can be an issue.
> Here is what I would do:
> Make the precision parameters of the beta distribution the same, i mean:  tau.beta1.lpsi = ... =  tau.beta5.lpsi =  tau.lpsi, also do the same for  the tau.betan.lp. This is a strong assumption that may not be true, but it is just a try to reduce the over parametrisation, and if the outcome is good, then we have now better starting values.
> Try to use a different non informative prior, maybe make it a bit informative. If the model is strong enough and reaches convergence it will update to the best posterior distribution.
> I think JAGS by default uses random walk sampler, maybe you can change this by doing block sampling, on your parameters \beta.lpsi and \beta.lp, you may have to be carefull with the correlation of the chains latter, but that is another issue.
> I hope this works, let me know.
>
> -

> > Dear Christoph,
> >
> > total non-mixing of the kind shown in your plots is sometimes due to an overparameterized model, i.e., when you try to squeeze more out of your data in terms of param estimates than what one can. So I was wondering whether perhaps you had in your model an intercept PLUS 5 parameters for the 5 habitat types. But that doesn't seem to be the case, so it can't be that. All the other covariates in the occupancy part of your model are continuous, right ? Nothing which represents two groups with two parameters (which then would lead to overparameterization) ?
> >
> > I don't think there is a lot that one could tune in JAGS. For that you have to go to Nimble. This should be easy since the basic model-definition language is practically the same as the BUGS dialect in JAGS. Might be worth a try.
> >
> > MCMC can be sensitive to parameterization of a model, i.e., how you specify a model in one of multiple equivalent ways. Sometimes miraculously one parameterization works much better than another. So that might be something that you could try. For instance, specify the occupancy part of the model as an intercept, plus 4 indicator variables for the differences of 4 habitat types relative to the baseline, plus the rest. Perhaps that leads to better mixing ?
> >
> > Yet another idea: sometimes one may have what appears like total lack of mixing, but then suddenly the chains make a jump and converge. If you haven't already run your model for, say, a week (and you can do that), then I would try that as well.
> >
> > All these are simply a blind chicken's try to find a grain. Somebody knowledgeable in MCMC might give more targeted advice.

messages.subject: Re: nimble - how to get error line number?
messages.subject_clean: nimble - how to get error line number?
messages.body_plain:
Dear Perry,

thanks for your kind explanation of this particular error! In my case, `k` wasn't stochastic, just a simple fixed number given in `data`. It helped to move it from `data` to `constants` and the error disappeared.

But my question was more general - how to get the line number of the error? It can be quite frustrating (hence the tone of my email, sorry and thanks for your kind answer :)) when you have a model code over several pages and you get an error you don't quite understand without any reference to particular line of code (or at least, to some node name). And if nimble is not capable of reporting line numbers yet, please consider this. It really solves time and nerves of the model developers :-)

Best wishes,

Tomas

On Sat, 27 Nov 2021 at 01:15, Perry de Valpine <pdeva...@berkeley.edu> wrote:
> Hi Tomas,
>
> Sorry to hear you're having a bumpy first experience using nimble.  Informative error-trapping can be difficult.  I understand your reaction.
>
> There is a nimble-users list (information at https://r-nimble.org/more/issues-and-groups).  You can post there for more support.  You will likely be asked to share your code, on-list if you don't mind, off-list if you prefer.
>
> What the error message is saying is that somewhere you have something like x[1:k] on the right-hand side of a model declaration (a line of model code), where k itself is declared as stochastic (meaning somewhere there is a "k ~ d<something>(...)".  Because nimble creates an internal representation of the graphical model relationships -- what depends on what -- a stochastically (aka dynamically) indexed vector is difficult to handle.   We say something is dynamically indexed if the index itself is a variable that might for example be sampled by MCMC.  Scalar dynamic indexing is easily supported, e.g. "y ~ dnorm(mu[k], sd = sigma)" where k is stochastic such as "k ~ dcat(probs[1:N])" so that k takes values in 1, 2, ... N.  The difficulty is vector dynamic indexing, like x[1:k].  The message is saying that a good way to accomplish that is by writing a nimbleFunction to use in the model, which simply means writing a function in a way that nimble can compile it.  For example, if you want
>
> sum_x <- sum(x[1:k]) # where k is stochastic
>
> you could instead do
>
> sum_x <- dynamic_sum(x[1:N], start = 1, end = k) # where N is static (given in the `constants` [or `data`] lists) and is the maximum possible value of k.
>
> dynamic_sum <- nimbleFunction(
>  run = function(x = double(1), start = double(), end = double()) { # declares x is a vector and start and end are scalars.  All values in models are double precision even if only integers are needed.
>    return(sum(x[start:end]))
>    returnType(double()) # return will be scalar
>  })
>
> Now, in the graphical model, sum_x will depend on all of x[1:N] and on k, and the nimbleFunction that calculates sum_x will return sum(x[1:k]).
>
> HTH
> -Perry
>
>
> On Fri, Nov 26, 2021 at 6:41 AM Tomas T. <tomas.t...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Dear all,
> >
> > I just started with nimble, converting my JAGS code to it. I am getting errors while compiling the model with the nimbleModel() function, but it doesn't give me any line numbers!  Like this:
> >
> > "Defining model
> > Error in getSymbolicParentNodesRecurse(x, constNames, indexNames, nimbleFunctionNames,  :
> >   Dynamic indexing found in a vector of indices, 1:k. Only scalar indices, such as 'idx' in 'x[idx]', can be dynamic. One can instead use dynamic indexing in a vector of indices inside a nimbleFunction."
> >
> > How do I get nimble to tell me the line number in the model code where problem occurs? I cannot believe that such already famous software would just let you debug like this, because that's quite unusable.
> >
> > Thanks a lot and best regards,
> >
> > Tomas

messages.subject: New R package "spOccupancy"
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am excited to announce our new R package "spOccupancy" is now available on CRAN <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/spOccupancy/index.html>. The package fits single-species, multi-species, and integrated spatially-explicit occupancy models in a Bayesian framework. We use efficient MCMC algorithms to ensure users can fit spatially-explicit models for potentially massive data sets (e.g., 100,000 locations).

spOccupancy provides functionality for data simulation, model fitting, model validation (by posterior predictive checks), model comparison (using WAIC and k-fold cross-validation), and prediction. For a detailed vignette and examples of the package's functionality, please see the package website <https://www.jeffdoser.com/files/spoccupancy-web/> as well as a recent preprint <https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.12163> that describes our methods in much more detail. I hope you find the package useful for your analyses, and please feel free to contact me with questions or issues.

Kind regards,

Jeff

messages.subject_clean: advert for the spOccupancy R package
messages.body_plain:
Dear all

over the holidays I've been exploring the new spOccupancy R package, which lets you fit spatial and non-spatial occupancy models to large and very large data sets (see https://www.jeffdoser.com/files/spoccupancy-web/). And I must say that it's really cool ! For map-making in the SDM business, accommodating spatial autocorrelation, i.e., fitting spatial models, can be a real plus. Now this can be done in JAGS, Nimble etc, but is much harder for the not-so-initiated. And: run times for spatial models can be huge and convergence rates terrible.

spOccupancy (along with only a very small handful other R packages, including stocc, hSDM and also the brand-new ubms) makes spatial occupancy modeling fairly easy even for beginners and lets you fit several types of occupancy models to even very large data sets overnight.

Here are some species distribution maps for the Rock bunting in Switzerland. I had detection/nondetection data from about 25k 1km2 quadrats (for a total modeled domain of 42k such quadrats). Original temporal resolution was 140 daily occasions, but R choked on that on my laptop, so I aggregated to weekly occasions. In occupancy I added 17 environmental predictors in both linear and squared form, and I had survey date in linear and squared form in detection. I fit a non-spatial model and then a spatial model with exponential spatial correlation and considering only 15 nearest-neighbours at each site (a significant comp/stats "trick" explained in more detail in the spOccupancy documentation). The non-spatial model ran in 5 hours, while the spatial model ran in 11. Convergence was good for the former and so-so for the latter (biggest Rhat was about 1.3, so if this were for a publication I would have run much longer). WAIC said that the spatial model was far better than the non-spatial model.

The maps on the left show predicted occupancy probability (posterior means) and its uncertainty (posterior standard deviations) from the non-spatial model. Comparing this map with the density map in the latest Swiss breeding bird atlas (Knaus et al. 2018), this SDM overpredicts a lot, showing moderate probabilities in a far too big region, while not showing the density centres well enough. In contrast, the spatial model (on the right) gets rid of a lot of the "unnecessary yellow" in the occupancy map and shows the real centres of the Swiss Rock bunting distribution in much sharper detail (albeit with more uncertainty). The reason for why the spatial model predicts so much better is the presence in the model of a spatial random field in occupancy, which is shown at the bottom right. You can think of this as a sort of spatially smeared out occupancy residual map, which corrects for differences between the observed data and what is predicted by the covariates alone.

Fitting this model in JAGS with splines to accommodate spatial autocorrelation might perhaps haven taken 2 weeks, so spOccupancy is a real asset if you want to fit spatial occupancy models especially to large data sets.

So I wish you good luck with your own spatial occupancy modeling !

Best regards  --- Marc

PS: Apologies for the long email ... and the heavy attachment 🙂

One of the simplest data types has got me stymied, for some reason. That data type is individual-level probabilities of connecting to each of the target populations (e.g., probabilities of breeding population assignment from nonbreeding genetic samples, where one is trying to estimate nonbreeding to breeding population-level transition probabilities). It seems like it should be easy - the data (probT) and parameter to be estimated (psi) are essentially the same thing, transition probabilities to target populations that sum to 1, either by individual or by origin population.
